extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (attorneys, agents), judges, and patentees interested in claim construction and drafting
extracted.subtask_description: Analysis of the doctrine of claim differentiation as applied in Retractable Technologies, with implications for claim construction and patent drafting (written description/enablement considerations).

rubrics_metrics.name: Doctrine of claim differentiation (presumption)
rubrics_metrics.description: “The presence of a dependent claim that adds a particular limitation gives rise to a presumption that the limitation in question is not present in the independent claim.” (Phillips v. AWH Corp.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the existence of a dependent claim that adds a limitation as creating a presumption that the independent claim does not include that limitation. The article repeatedly treats this as a baseline canon of claim construction and a check against importing limitations from dependent claims into independent claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Strength of the claim-differentiation presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: Chief Judge Rader: the presumption is a “strong presumption”; Judge Lourie: the implication “is not a strong one.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The presumption is especially strong when the limitation in dispute is the only meaningful difference between an independent and dependent claim and one party is urging that the limitation be read into the independent claim (citing SunRace Roots). Whether the presumption is 'strong' can be dispositive in claim construction disputes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on importing limitations from dependent to independent claims
rubrics_metrics.description: One should not read limitations recited in a dependent claim into the independent claim absent strong reason; importing such limitations is disfavored.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: applying the dependent claim’s limitation to the independent claim without overcoming the claim-differentiation presumption. The article criticizes reading the dependent claim’s 'one-piece' limitation into the independent claim in Retractable Technologies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Read claim language in view of the written description/specification
rubrics_metrics.description: “The claim language must always be read in view of the written description” (Phillips).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification that repeatedly characterizes the invention in limiting terms (e.g., 'one piece hollow body', 'each syringe embodiment contains a one-piece') can be used to construe claim terms more narrowly. Courts will consider specification statements, prior-art discussion, and how embodiments are described when construing claim terms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims themselves define the claimed invention; ordinary and customary meaning
rubrics_metrics.description: The claims themselves, not the written description portion of the specification, define the claimed invention; claim language is to be given its ordinary and customary meaning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a term has no special technical meaning and parties do not contend otherwise, construction may require ‘little more than the application of the widely accepted meaning of commonly understood words.’ This supports resisting narrow constructions not supported by claim language.

rubrics_metrics.name: When specification can rebut the claim-differentiation presumption
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification that (1) disparages alternatives as prior art, (2) explicitly states the invention features a particular limited structure, and (3) describes each embodiment as containing the limitation, may rebut the presumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Lourie relied on the 'Summary of the Invention' stating 'one piece hollow body', prior-art characterization, and that 'the specifications do not disclose a body that consists of multiple pieces' to justify limiting claim term 'body' to one-piece. Use of such specification language is a path for rebuttal, but must be weighed against the presumption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting guideline: exemplify alternative embodiments to avoid narrow constructions
rubrics_metrics.description: Patent applicants should specifically exemplify alternative embodiments (e.g., multi-piece body) in the specification to avoid narrow constructions that import limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical drafting tip from the article: explicitly describe embodiments that cover the alternative structures you want the claims to encompass. Failure to exemplify alternatives can create vulnerability to a narrow construction or enablement challenges.

rubrics_metrics.name: Drafting guideline: avoid limiting statements in the Summary of the Invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid language in the Summary of the Invention that could be read as limiting, such as repeatedly stating the invention 'features a one piece hollow body.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The article notes that limiting references in the Summary can create a faulty presumption in judges' minds that the claimed invention is limited by those descriptions—drafters should use careful, non-limiting phrasing in summaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enablement risk under 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph
rubrics_metrics.description: Not specifically exemplifying certain embodiments (e.g., multi-piece bodies) may create enablement issues under 35 U.S.C. § 112, first paragraph.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to disclose or exemplify claimed variations could give rise to a potential lack-of-enablement argument. The article flags enablement as a possible risk when alternative embodiments are not described.

rubrics_metrics.name: Written-description and indefiniteness considerations (35 U.S.C. § 112)
rubrics_metrics.description: Claim construction disputes may implicate written-description requirements and possibly indefiniteness under 35 U.S.C. § 112.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge Plager focused on concerns about 'indefinite and ambiguous claims, divorced from the written description' and suggested the need for stringent rules; drafters and courts should be mindful that ambiguous claim language divorced from specification support can trigger §112 issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordinary-meaning fallback where no special technical meaning exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If no party contends that a claim term has a special technical meaning, construction should default to the ordinary and customary meaning of the word (e.g., 'body' not limited to 'one-piece' absent other indications).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is a corollary to the 'claims define the invention' principle: courts should not construe ordinary words narrowly unless the specification or context clearly demands it.
